articles.headline: Gold for Peru: Piccolo Clemente is the world longboard champion
articles.standfirst: The Peruvian surfer won his second world title at a beach in El Salvador.
body: The Peruvian surfer Benoit 'Piccolo' Clemente is the new longboard world champion. He won the 2026 ISA World Longboard Championship at El Sunzal beach in El Salvador. Everyone in Peruvian sport is very proud of the champion.
In the men's final, Piccolo scored 17.30 points. Tony Silvagni from the United States came second with 16.10 points, and Edouard Delpero from France came third with 15.73 points.
This is Piccolo's second world title. He won his first one in 2019. The Peruvian team also did very well and won a bronze medal. France was first and the United States was second.

The president of the Peruvian Institute of Sport, Óscar Fernández Cáceres, congratulated Piccolo. Now the surfer is getting ready for the Pan American Games in Lima in 2027. Many people in Peru are very happy with his result.

articles.headline: Happy sounds and tasty treats: what orangutans chose
articles.standfirst: A new study says that orangutans like food linked to the sound of laughter.
body: Scientists have studied orangutans, big apes with red-orange hair. They wanted to know if happy sounds can change how animals learn.
The team worked with six orangutans in two zoos. First, they taught the animals to look in bowls for a tasty treat. The treat was hidden under moss or sawdust.
Before each test, the animals heard a recording. Sometimes it was the sound of orangutans playing and laughing. Sometimes it was only the wind.
At the end, the orangutans could choose between two bowls. Most of them chose the bowl with the material linked to the laughing sound. Four of the six showed a clear choice.
The scientists think that happy feelings can change what an animal remembers. They also think the idea may help us understand how people learn.

articles.headline: A safe for seeds at the end of the world: Peru sends its crops to Norway
articles.standfirst: Quinoa, kiwicha and chili peppers from Peru are now stored in the Svalbard 'Noah's Ark'.
body: Deep under the ground on the island of Spitsbergen, in Norway's Svalbard islands, there is a cold, safe place that people sometimes call 'Noah's Ark'. It is the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, and its job is to keep seeds safe in case of a disaster or a food shortage anywhere in the world. This week, it received a new delivery from Peru.

Peru's National Institute for Agrarian Innovation, known as INIA, sent 71 types of food crops. There were 46 kinds of kiwicha, 20 of quinoa, four of chili pepper and one of tomato. Quinoa and kiwicha are native Peruvian crops, and they are famous for being very nutritious.

It was the second shipment under an agreement between the governments of Peru and Norway. The vault is paid for by the Norwegian government and is more than 100 metres underground, so natural or human-made disasters should not reach it. Christian Barrantes Bravo, the director of INIA, said the delivery shows how important Peru and its biodiversity are for future food supplies.

Barrantes also explained that INIA works with the International Potato Center to keep a reserve of native plant material and to improve crops such as potatoes and purple corn. One purple corn variety, called Negro Canaán, has a lot of anthocyanin, a natural antioxidant. Thanks to these improvements, Peru can now export the corn cobs and the anthocyanin separately.

articles.headline: One small step for Australia? A country offers its own astronaut to the space station
articles.standfirst: The government has asked the European Space Agency to send Katherine Bennell-Pegg to space in 2028.
body: Australia has sent an offer to the European Space Agency (ESA) to put one of its own astronauts on the International Space Station. The astronaut is Katherine Bennell-Pegg, who is also the Australian of the Year. If the mission goes ahead in 2028, she will be the first qualified astronaut to fly to space under the Australian flag.

Australia has had astronauts before, but they travelled in a different way. Andy Thomas and Paul Scully-Power were born in Australia, but they went to space as US citizens on NASA missions. Elaine Hyde, who has both Australian and US citizenship, took a short flight into space last year with Blue Origin, a private company.

Bennell-Pegg is the director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency, and she finished her astronaut training with the ESA in 2024. A space trip is very expensive, and the science minister, Tim Ayres, has said that no government could pay for it alone. Some people who give money to good causes have promised more than $6 million in cash, and some state governments have shown interest in helping. South Australia, where the agency has its headquarters, says it is ready to support the plan.
The government also says the trip would be a complete Australian mission, with experiments and technology that were developed in Australia.

articles.headline: Custom-made against cancer: a personal vaccine shows promise for melanoma patients
articles.standfirst: An Australian-led trial suggests that a vaccine designed for each patient can cut the risk of the disease coming back.
body: A vaccine designed for one patient at a time has, for the first time, given positive results in a large late-stage cancer trial. The treatment, called intismeran, is aimed at melanoma, a serious form of skin cancer. It works by teaching the immune system to attack changes in the genes that are unique to each person's tumour.

The trial was led from Australia and involved 1,137 patients at 157 sites around the world. All of them had already had their melanoma removed by surgery, but they were at high risk of the disease returning. For twelve months, every patient received an immunotherapy drug called pembrolizumab, and some were also given the personalised vaccine.

Two years later, the combination had reduced the risk of the cancer coming back, or of death, by 42% compared with the drug alone. Among the patients who received both treatments, 82% were alive and free of the disease, against 70% of those who had only pembrolizumab.

Professor Georgina Long, of the Melanoma Institute Australia, described the findings as 'a foundational shift' in the approach to cancer, because the vaccine uses the body's own defences in a more personalised way. Dr Jessamy Tiffen, who was not involved in the research, pointed out that earlier therapies usually targeted a single gene change, whereas this vaccine aims at up to 34 mutations in each patient.

There are reasons to stay cautious, however. The results will be presented at a cancer conference in Madrid this weekend and have been accepted by a leading medical journal, but they still have to be peer reviewed. The study was a phase III trial, the kind of large test that regulators require before a medicine can be approved for general use.

articles.headline: Colour under threat: most shallow coral reefs are now 'critically endangered'
articles.standfirst: The first global assessment of reef ecosystems gives a stark warning, but scientists say the reefs are not yet lost.
body: Coral reefs are famous for their colour and their abundance of life. Now, for the first time, experts have assessed the world's shallow-water reefs as ecosystems, and the result is alarming: 96% of them have been classified as critically endangered.

The assessment comes from the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and its Red List of Ecosystems. Scientists divided the reefs into 127 regions, according to their location and the species found there. Among the regions in the most serious category are the Great Barrier Reef off Australia, the Coral Triangle in the western Pacific, the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System in the Caribbean and the reefs of Florida.

'Critically endangered' does not mean that the reefs have already gone. It means that they face a very high risk of collapse within 50 years. The IUCN defines collapse as the near or complete loss of living hard corals, which leaves a reef unable to sustain itself. The main cause, the experts say, is heat stress linked to climate change, driven mostly by burning oil, gas and coal.

The stakes are high. According to scientists' estimates, shallow reefs support about a quarter of ocean species at some point in their life cycle, and hundreds of millions of people depend on them for fish and for protection along their coasts. Because of this, losing the reefs would affect much more than the sea creatures that live among the corals.

The researchers stressed that the future is not fixed. Their conclusion is based on the current path of climate change and on present greenhouse gas emissions. If countries do more to slow global warming, the outlook for reefs could improve. In other words, the assessment is a warning about a risk, not a final verdict.

articles.headline: A fruit in a genetic trap: can breeders save the world's favourite banana?
articles.standfirst: Disease threatens the Cavendish, and researchers are racing to replace it or rebuild it.
body: The banana in your fruit bowl is almost certainly a Cavendish, and that is precisely the problem. Cavendish bananas have three sets of chromosomes, which makes them sterile; combined with their ability to produce fruit without pollination, this gives us the seedless fruit we know. Growers multiply the plants from offshoots, so each one is virtually a genetic copy of its parent. The result is wonderfully uniform fruit, and a crop that is uniformly vulnerable to the same diseases.

History has been here before. The Cavendish took over from the Gros Michel, a variety that fell victim to Panama disease from the 1950s. Now the Cavendish itself is under threat from a strain called Tropical Race 4, or TR4. According to Dr Jose De Vega, of the Earlham Institute in Norwich, it has spread from south-east Asia to Australia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America, and the most worrying recent report came from Ecuador, the world's largest banana exporter, in December 2025.

Researchers are pursuing several routes. This month, Yelloway, a collaboration between the banana company Chiquita and the crop-improvement firm KeyGene, announced a fully fertile Cavendish. In principle, that makes cross-breeding possible, and with it new varieties that are both commercially viable and resistant to disease. Chiquita's sustainability director, Peter Stedman, is frank about the aim: 'We are not trying to preserve Cavendish.' The company wants to replace it, arguing that genetic diversity lies at the core of any sustainable farming system.

Others favour a different technique. At Queensland University of Technology, Professor James Dale's team used a bacterium to insert a gene from a wild banana that resists TR4. The result, called QCAV-4, has been approved for human consumption in Australia and New Zealand, and researchers say it tastes like the traditional fruit. De Vega, meanwhile, is working with colleagues on gene editing, which alters the Cavendish's own DNA so that it matches the version of a gene found in resistant varieties.

The stakes reach far beyond the breakfast table. The world grows about 139 million tonnes of bananas a year, and the fruit is a staple food and a source of income for millions of people in the tropics, from Guatemala to Malawi.

articles.headline: Counting the unseen: Europe's summer heat may have killed far more than records show
articles.standfirst: New estimates suggest that more than 50,000 people died in a single summer, and that climate change tripled the toll.
body: Official figures rarely capture the full human cost of a heat wave, and this week scientists in London tried to fill the gap. In a pair of peer-reviewed studies published in Nature Health, researchers estimated that severe heat killed more than 50,000 people in European cities and towns this summer. If the estimate is right, it was by far the deadliest summer of the century so far for the continent.

The team did not rely on death reports. Instead, they combined factors that shape heat-related health risks in each place, among them the age of the population, socioeconomic indicators and the availability of health services. This matters because governments usually count deaths from heatstroke but not necessarily those from heart and breathing problems that extreme temperatures make worse, so the true toll of a heat wave is often underreported.

The central finding concerns climate change. According to the studies, about three times as many people died as would have done had humankind not warmed the planet by burning oil, gas and coal. Large parts of Europe endured a series of heat domes, sprawling weather systems that allow heat to build up for days on end, and the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases pushed temperatures during such events even higher.

Clair Barnes, a climate scientist at Imperial College London and lead author of both studies, was careful not to overstate the case. Even in a preindustrial climate, she said, some of these heat waves would have caused high mortality; but human-caused warming, mainly from fossil fuels, pushed it substantially higher. Her point is that the two causes cannot be separated neatly: the weather and the warming acted together.

Estimates of this kind come with caveats, because they model what probably happened rather than counting individual cases. Even so, they offer a fuller picture than official statistics alone, and they underline a point that is easy to miss: the danger of a heat wave is often invisible, hidden among deaths from illnesses that the heat made worse. Anyone who plans for future heat waves, therefore, needs to look beyond the official numbers.

cartoons.title: Wonderful news

image.alt: Four panels: Bea reads a message from Max, Byte takes it literally, Bea explains sarcasm, and Byte updates his dictionary.

transcript.speaker: Bea
transcript.text: Max says, 'No worries! I loved waiting forty minutes for you.'

transcript.speaker: Bea
transcript.text: Byte, that is sarcasm. I owe him an apology and a very large snack.

transcript.speaker: Byte
transcript.text: Updating dictionary: 'loved' sometimes means 'did not love'.

cartoons.explanation: Max writes the opposite of what he feels: he says he loved waiting, but he is really annoyed. Byte reads only the words and misses the tone. His final dictionary update is funny because it turns sarcasm into a neat rule, as if the meaning of a word could simply be reversed.

glossary.def: Saying the opposite of what you mean in order to show annoyance or to mock.
An informal way of saying that something is not a problem.
I should say sorry to him.

cartoons.prompt: B2: Why does Max's message seem polite but feel unfriendly? Rewrite it as a sincere message in 40–60 words. C1: Explain how tone and context change the meaning of the words in the first panel, and why Byte's last remark is both logical and inadequate (70–100 words).
cartoons.discussion: A possible reading is that Byte is not entirely wrong: words do shift meaning with context, and his dictionary note records that. What he lacks is the social judgement that tells us which meaning applies. The strip also hints at Bea's responsibility: Max's sarcasm is a polite-looking way of expressing a real grievance, so the best reply is an apology, not a lesson in vocabulary.
